description:
Why Can't You Ever Go Faster Than Light?

Episode 69 of a daily journey through the universe. ⚡
The speed of light: almost 300,000 km per second. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us, Andromeda's light 2.5 million years. Why looking far away means looking back in time, and why nothing with mass can reach it.

segments.text: Why can't anything go faster than light? Not you, not a rocket, not anything.
Light travels at almost three hundred thousand kilometers every second.
That's fast enough to go around Earth more than seven times in one second.
Moonlight takes just over one second to reach you. Sunlight takes about eight minutes.
segments.headline: 8 minutes from the Sun

segments.text: So when you look at the Sun, you see it as it was eight minutes ago. If it vanished, you wouldn't know for eight minutes.
segments.headline: Looking into the past

segments.text: The light from the Andromeda galaxy left it two and a half million years ago, before modern humans existed.
segments.headline: 2.5 million years ago

segments.text: So telescopes are time machines. The farther we look, the further back in time we see.
segments.headline: Telescopes are time machines

segments.text: In nineteen oh five, Einstein showed that nothing with mass can reach the speed of light. The faster you go, the harder it gets to speed up.
segments.headline: The ultimate limit

segments.text: Our fastest spacecraft, the Parker Solar Probe, has reached about two hundred kilometers per second. Still less than one tenth of one percent of light speed.
segments.headline: Our fastest spacecraft
